content: NHS Primary Care Trusts (PCTs) are statutory organizations in England that form part of the National Health Service (NHS). They are tasked with delivering healthcare services and improving health outcomes within their designated local areas. These trusts evolved from committees or Primary Care Groups that were previously part of the former Health Authorities. PCTs are responsible for managing approximately 80% of the total NHS budget. Each PCT operates with its own budget and sets its own priorities, but these must align with the overarching priorities and budgets established by the relevant Strategic Health Authority (SHA) and the Department of Health. PCTs directly provide a variety of community health services. They allocate funding for general practitioners (GPs) and medical prescriptions. Additionally, they commission hospital and mental health services from appropriate NHS trusts or private sector providers. This commissioning role makes them comparable to payers in the United States healthcare system. Current government policies anticipate that at least 15% of services will eventually be commissioned from private or voluntary sectors. Furthermore, the direct services currently provided by PCTs are expected to be commissioned on an arm's length basis in the future. PCTs are managed by a team of Executive Directors, led by a Chief Executive. These directors are members of the Trust's Board, which also includes non-executive directors appointed through an open advertisement process. The Chairman of the Trust is a non-executive director. Other board members may include representatives from the Trust's Professional Executive Committee (PEC), which is composed of elected local GPs, community nurses, pharmacists, dentists, and other healthcare professionals. From October 2006, the Chair of the Audit Committee of PCTs has also been appointed through an open advertisement process, rather than being selected by the Board from among the non-executive directors. The financial and operational agenda of PCTs is largely determined by directives from the Strategic Health Authority or the Department of Health. In 2005, the Government announced plans to reduce the number of Strategic Health Authorities and PCTs, with the latter being reduced by approximately 50%. As a result, as of October 1, 2006, the number of PCTs in England was reduced from 303 to 152, with each PCT serving an average population of just under 330,000. Only the PCTs in London retained their original boundaries. Following these changes, around 70% of PCTs became co-terminous with local authorities that have social service responsibilities. This alignment is intended to facilitate joint planning between health and social care services. Additionally, it is anticipated that these mergers will generate approximately £259 million in annual savings for the NHS.
